Re-Examining the "Out of Africa" theory. Any thoughts on this? Looks interesting.

Ah, yes, this is that Russian guy/guys.

After a careful reading when I saw this over a year ago, it seems like a stretch / he may not be (pretty likely isn't) right. That's OK, because it keeps the conversation going. It's always valuable to re-examine "consensus" as you can discover new things.

An important thing to remember is that there was some original population that came from somewhere, and that pretty much had to be Africa. Then the populations diverged into three major groups, and some minor ones. (Neandertal, Denisovan, and the archaic Homo S. that remained in Africa). Various populations of hominids didn't just spring forth into existence in multiple places. The original, archaic ancestor population had to come from somewhere. So then these researchers have to explain how the later transformation to more modern populations somehow has matching genetic fingerprints that look like mixing, as "drift" in different populations producing matching SNPs and loci in various places need explaning.
Their explanation although some parts of it might be correct, just didn't seem right overall, as it doesn't "match" what we think happened from studying all sorts of other parts of the puzzle.
Coming up with an alternative to the "2nd migration out of Africa" hypothesis is pretty tough. Saying it happened much earlier, that's not so tough. His abstract looks sound, but then when you get down into the details, it looks like there are some conclusions that don't really follow.
